newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine stocks seen riding out graft scandal.
newsitem.headline: Argentine stocks seen riding out graft scandal.

text.p: Argentina's new corruption controversy may jar some nerves on the bolsa, but will not cause lasting damage, analysts say.
The public debate on government graft, stoked by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, is long overdue and could actually be welcomed abroad as a sign of political progress, observers say.

Moreover, President Carlos Menem's quick jump on the anti-corruption bandwagon has snatched the spotlight from the opposition and could restore his popularity, now at an all-time low, in time for next year's mid-term elections -- ultimately boosting the markets.
"The key point is that the government has seized this as an issue for the first time," said Frank McGann, vice president at Merrill Lynch in Buenos Aires.

The bolsa's blue-chip MerVal index, which has risen for seven consecutive weeks, slipped 1.8 percent in early trading Tuesday, unsettled by accusations of corruption hurled by Cavallo against two cabinet ministers.
But stocks pared losses to less than half by the close and traders said harm from corruption talk would be limited.

"We've had some shocking news recently, starting with the customs scandal, and everyone's a bit edgy," said Juan Pablo Paillot at local traders Rabello, referring to an alleged smuggling ring now being investigated by authorities. The ring reportedly caused a loss $3 billion in government revenues.
"But for now I think the political rumors have been pretty much digested and we're heading for a slight bounce, with steady buying by the pension funds," he added.

Cavallo Tuesday told Argentine radio from New York that Interior Minister Carlos Corach and Justice Minister Elias Jassan had often meddled in court investigations and even prided themselves in hand-picking prosecutors and judges.
Corach denied the charges and said he would take legal action, while Jassan said he would not immediately respond to Cavallo's accusations.

The former minister, sacked by President Carlos Menem July 26 after a running battle with ruling Peronist party hardliners, had first denounced government-linked "mafias" in customs and postal services more than one year ago.
At the time, his charges were resisted by Menem, who suddenly changed tack this month and launched his own crusade against corruption in the wake of the customs scandal.
Analysts said the trading of accusations between Corach and Cavallo could bring back memories of the old government clashes which typically rattled the markets.

"This is not the same old argument between Menem and Cavallo," said analyst Raul Buonuome of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "First of all, Cavallo's no longer in the government -- we just have to get used to seeing him in the political arena, which these days means talking corruption."

"But what's really interesting, what's different, is that Cavallo and Menem have taken the fight against corruption away from the opposition, so that even if there are repercussions, the overall performance of the market shouldn't suffer."
And these days Cavallo's outbursts no longer cast doubt on the future of convertibility or fiscal targets.

"The markets aren't worried about a debate which has clear political connotations and raises no questions about the continuation of economic policy," said Buonuome. "What foreign investors are really worried about are things like labor reforms, which seem to be making good progress."
